title: Conceptual Models
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Conceptual Models.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A conceptual model is the product’s designed explanation of what exists in the system, how those things relate, and what actions can change them. It is the bridge between the underlying technical system and the person’s mental model. Strong conceptual models make state, object relationships, and consequences predictable across the product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Define the core objects, their attributes, their possible states, and the actions available to people. Then make these choices visible through language, navigation, controls, and feedback. A conceptual model is not an internal database schema; it is the useful explanation that lets people reason about the product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at specify the designed world?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Define the core objects, relationships, actions, states, rules, and vocabulary people must understand. Keep this model coherent across navigation, content, controls, data, and channels. A “project” cannot behave like a folder in one place and a permission group elsewhere without explanation.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Compare the conceptual model with people’s mental models and the implementation model. Expose distinctions that change action while hiding technical detail that does not. Use object and state diagrams, scenarios, and prototype prediction tasks to find contradictions before visual polish distributes them.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at test coherence, not recognition?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Apply the model across navigation, messages, service channels, and time. If the dashboard calls something a “case,” email calls it a “request,” and phone staff call it a “referral,” establish whether these are synonyms or different objects. If “cancel” is reversible in one place and final in another, the verb is not coherent.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Prototype tests should ask people to predict: If you change this slot, what remains? If the clinic asks for information, is the referral lost? Who can see this preparation note? What would you expect after cancelling? Errors reveal model contradictions earlier than preference questions do.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Define the model as objects, actions, relationships, and rules
turns.text: What changes when we look at define the model as objects, actions, relationships, and rules?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team tests it through scenarios: two offers, withdrawn request, changed clinic, delegated helper, stale availability, and uncertain delivery. Interface, content, service, data, and analytics must express the same distinctions. When teams cannot explain a state without exceptions, the model—not only the label—needs revision.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Make the product's concepts coherent across channels
turns.text: What changes when we look at make the product's concepts coherent across channels?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Simplicity comes from removing unnecessary concepts or making relationships intelligible, not from concealing consequential state. The team tests whether people can predict outcomes, explain current state, and recover from exceptions. A coherent conceptual model reduces the amount of interface explanation needed because every new encounter builds on the same underlying logic.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Inconsistency is often a model problem, not a component problem. Before standardising screens, examine whether teams disagree about what the product’s objects and states actually mean.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A conceptual model is the product’s deliberate explanation of what exists, how things relate, what actions are possible, and what causes change. It gives an experience its internal logic. In an email product, for example, the model may include messages, threads, labels, folders, archives, drafts, recipients, and actions such as send, reply, delete, or restore.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: When these objects and actions behave consistently, people can make useful predictions even before they know every feature.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Make the model explicit before producing individual screens. Define core objects, attributes, relationships, lifecycle states, permissions, and action consequences. Check it against users’ mental models and the service’s underlying rules.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A coherent model makes navigation, content, error messages, interaction patterns, and data structures easier to align; an incoherent one pushes complexity into labels, exceptions, and training.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Screen-first design: controls are designed before the product’s objects and relationships are understood. Inconsistent verbs: the same action word produces different outcomes in different places. Hidden state: people cannot tell what object they are acting on or what state it is in.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metaphor leakage: a familiar metaphor is used beyond the point where the underlying system behaves like it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: In a project tool, is a task a document, a conversation, a status, or an object that moves through a workflow? If the product cannot answer coherently, every new screen teaches a different rule.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Mental models belong to people; conceptual models belong to the design. lesson 16 examines one tool designers use to connect them: metaphor.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Describe how a product “thinks” in one sentence. Then test your claim against a different screen or workflow in the same product.
